epithets.name: el Buen Conde
epithets.note: The Good Count: the standing formula of the Poema de Fernán González, which uses it thirty-three times, and a literary title rather than a contemporary one.

summary: Count of Castile from about 931 to 970 who united the Leonese frontier counties into one lordship and made it hereditary in his family, and whom later legend turned into the founder of Castilian independence.
details: Fernán González commanded the eastern march of León against Córdoba, fought at the Battle of Simancas, repopulated Sepúlveda, and rebelled against Ramiro II and his successors often enough to be imprisoned twice. His son inherited the county in 970 without a royal appointment, which is the real measure of what he achieved.
overview: Fernán González was count of Castile from about 931 until his death in 970, and the first man to hold the whole eastern march of the Kingdom of León as a single command. He gathered the separate counties of Burgos, Lara, Álava, Cerezo and Lantarón into one hand, fought the Caliphate of Córdoba on the Duero frontier, rebelled twice against his own kings and was imprisoned for it, and left the county to his son without asking León’s permission.

That last fact is the substance of his reputation: Castile became hereditary under him, which in practice made it autonomous. The independence that later Castilians credited him with is another matter. It is first claimed in a chronicle written two centuries after his death and elaborated in the Poema de Fernán González, the monastic epic that gave him the bargain of the horse and the hawk, and no document of his own century supports it.
greatestFeats: United Burgos, Lara, Álava, Cerezo and Lantarón into a single county of Castile
Fought in the Christian victory at the Battle of Simancas in 939
Repopulated Sepúlveda and granted it a fuero in 940
Made the county hereditary: his son García Fernández succeeded him in 970

birth.note: Son of Gonzalo Fernández, count of Burgos and Castile, and Muniadona, whose name Andalusi writers later used for the Castilian comital line.

death.circumstance: He confirms charters for the last time in August 969 and his son appears as count on 20 February 970, so he died between those dates; he was buried at the monastery of San Pedro de Arlanza.

quickFacts.knownFor: Uniting the Castilian counties and making the county hereditary

contentSections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Fernán González was count of Castile from about 931 until his death in 970, and the first man to hold the whole eastern march of the Kingdom of León as a single command. He gathered the separate counties of Burgos, Lara, Álava, Cerezo and Lantarón into one hand, fought the Caliphate of Córdoba on the Duero frontier, rebelled twice against his own kings and was imprisoned for it, and left the county to his son without asking León’s permission.

That last fact is the substance of his reputation: Castile became hereditary under him, which in practice made it autonomous. The independence that later Castilians credited him with is another matter. It is first claimed in a chronicle written two centuries after his death and elaborated in the Poema de Fernán González, the monastic epic that gave him the bargain of the horse and the hawk, and no document of his own century supports it.

contentSections.title: Birth and early life
paragraphs: He was born about 910 at the castle of Lara, in the upland country south-east of Burgos, to Count Gonzalo Fernández and his wife Muniadona. His father had been made count of Burgos around 899 and count of Castile about 909, and had begun putting back together a frontier command that had been broken up after the death of Diego Rodríguez Porcelos in 885.

Castile at this date was not a country and not even one county. It was the eastern march of the Kingdom of León, a belt of repopulated valleys and castles — the castella that gave it its name — held by several counts at once, each appointed by the Leonese king and removable by him. When Gonzalo died in 915 the counties passed in turn to Fernando Ansúrez, to Gonzalo’s brother Nuño Fernández, to Fernando Ansúrez again and to Gutier Núñez. Fernán González grew up inside that instability and spent his career ending it.

contentSections.title: Character and Personality
paragraphs: The contemporary evidence for his character is thin and hostile in tone. Sampiro, writing in León within living memory, says that in 944 Fernán González and Diego Muñoz "exercised tyranny against King Ramiro and even prepared war", and that the king, being strong and foresighted, seized them and put them in irons. That is the voice of the court he defied: a great magnate who could not be trusted and had to be broken and then bought back with a royal marriage. His own charters show the other face of the same man — a lord endowing Arlanza and Cardeña, granting a fuero to settlers on the most exposed ground in Iberia, and building the alliances with Pamplona that his two marriages sealed.

The admiring portrait is entirely later and entirely literary. The Poema de Fernán González, written at San Pedro de Arlanza in the middle of the thirteenth century, calls him the buen conde thirty-three times and gives him the whole repertoire of the epic hero: visions of Saint Millán and Saint Pelayo, a hermit’s prophecy, escapes from prison contrived by his wife, and a stubborn refusal to be anybody’s vassal. The Primera Crónica General and the ballads took their Fernán González from there, and so, for six centuries, did Castile.

Modern historians read the two against each other and generally land on a third figure: an exceptionally able frontier politician rather than either a traitor or a liberator. He changed sides between León, Pamplona and Córdoba as the balance moved, lost as often as he won — imprisoned by one king and captured by another — and converted a revocable office into a family possession without ever once claiming a title he did not hold. Those who have written most sharply about the legend, including the historians of the mythification of Castilian origins, point out that the man in the documents never calls himself anything grander than comes, count.

contentSections.title: Making one county out of many
paragraphs: He appears with the title of count at Lara in 929, though documents naming him before 932 may be later confections. The decisive year was 931 or 932. Ramiro II of León came to the throne in November 931, and a charter of the monastery of San Pedro de Cardeña dated 932 records the new arrangement in a single line: Regnante Ranimiro in Obeto et comite Fredinando Gundissalbiz in Castella — Ramiro reigning in Oviedo and Count Fernando González in Castile.

In the same period Álvaro Herraméliz, count of Álava, Cerezo and Lantarón, died, and Fernán González took his counties and married his widow. Sancha Sánchez was a daughter of Sancho Garcés I of Pamplona and the formidable Queen Toda, and had already been married to King Ordoño II of León; the match made the Castilian count a member of the Navarrese royal family and gave him a standing no previous frontier count had enjoyed. By the middle of the 930s one man held every county from the Cantabrian coast to the Duero.

contentSections.title: The frontier war
paragraphs: Castile’s eastern march was the shortest road from Córdoba to the Christian north, and Fernán González spent his working life on it. Abd al-Rahman III devastated Álava, burned Burgos and sacked the monastery of Cardeña in 934; the count campaigned with Ramiro II in the relief of San Esteban de Gormaz and in the fighting around Osma.

In August 939 he fought in the Christian coalition that broke the caliph’s great muster at the Battle of Simancas, and in the pursuit that followed the Andalusi army was cut to pieces at a ravine the Arabic sources call the Alhandega, losing the caliph’s own equipment and copy of the Qur’an. Abd al-Rahman never again led an army in person.

He turned the victory into territory. In 940 he took and repopulated Sepúlveda beyond the Duero and granted it a fuero — a charter of liberties designed to attract settlers to ground nobody would otherwise farm, and the ancestor of the Castilian frontier charters that followed. A further Castilian victory over Andalusi troops at San Esteban de Gormaz is recorded in 955; in 963, after the town was destroyed again, he made terms with the caliph al-Hakam II and acted from then on with little reference to León.

contentSections.title: Rebellion, prison and the price of it
paragraphs: His relations with his own kings were worse than his relations with the caliph. Ramiro II placed the frontier garrisons under royal men and created a county at Monzón under Ansur Fernández, blocking Castilian expansion westward; in 944 Fernán González and Count Diego Muñoz of Saldaña rose against him. Ramiro took them both, stripped Castile from Fernán González, gave it to his own son the infante Sancho with Ansur Fernández as guardian, and held the count in irons at León.

He was released after a period the sources give differently — about a year in the Castilian accounts, three in others — on renewed oaths of fidelity, and the peace was sealed by marrying his daughter Urraca to Ramiro’s heir Ordoño. The reconciliation cost him nothing permanent: he had the county back and a granddaughter’s claim on the Leonese throne.

When Ramiro II died in 951 the kingdom fell into a dynastic quarrel that suited him exactly. He backed Sancho the Fat against Ordoño III, then recognised Ordoño when the rising failed, then abandoned Sancho for the rival Ordoño IV, who married the same daughter Urraca. In 960 the Navarrese intervened on Sancho’s behalf and Fernán González was defeated and taken prisoner by his own former brother-in-law, García Sánchez I of Pamplona, at Cirueña. He bought his freedom with territorial concessions and, about 964, with a second marriage to García’s daughter Urraca Garcés.

contentSections.title: Death and burial
paragraphs: He confirms royal charters for the last time in August 969, and on 20 February 970 a diploma is dated by the reign of Ramiro III in León and by Count García Fernández in Castile. He died between those two dates; Castilian tradition settled on 970.

The succession is the point. García Fernández took the county as his father’s heir, not as a royal appointee, and held it until 995, and the counts of Castile were a dynasty from then on. Fernán González was buried at San Pedro de Arlanza, the monastery he had endowed since the 930s and the house that would later write his legend. When the monastery was abandoned after the suppressions of the nineteenth century his sarcophagus and his first wife’s were moved, in 1841, to the collegiate church of Covarrubias, where the inscription calls him sovereign count of Castile — a title no document of his lifetime gives him.

contentSections.title: The poem, the horse and the hawk
paragraphs: The Poema de Fernán González was written between about 1250 and 1271 by a monk of San Pedro de Arlanza, in the cuaderna vía of the learned clerical poets: 762 stanzas, of which one incomplete fifteenth-century manuscript at El Escorial survives. Its purpose was double — to promote the tomb cult at Arlanza, and to supply the newly reunited crown of Castile with a founder who had been free of León from the start.

Its most famous episode is the sale of a horse and a goshawk. The count sells them to the king of León, and the price is to double for every day it goes unpaid; the king forgets, the debt compounds, and by the time it is reckoned the sum is larger than the kingdom can raise, so León releases Castile from its dependence in settlement. It is a good story about compound interest and a better one about national feeling, and there is no trace of it in any tenth-century source.

The independence itself is almost as literary. No document from the county records a separation from León, and the first surviving claim that Fernán González took the Castilians out of the Leonese yoke comes from the Crónica najerense, written around two hundred years after his death, which introduces it with the words "so it is said". Even the bronze Virgen de las Batallas at Burgos, the little image tradition says he carried on his saddle, is Limoges work of the thirteenth century and cannot have been his.

contentSections.title: Legacy
paragraphs: What he actually did was change the terms on which Castile was held. A county that had been an office in the king’s gift became a patrimony passed from father to son, defended by a family with its own marriages into Pamplona, its own monasteries, its own charters to its own settlers, and its own treaties with Córdoba. Everything that followed — Sancho III of Castile’s kingdom, the rise of the Castilian crown over León, the language and law the crown carried — began from a frontier command that stopped taking orders.

The legend then did work of its own. Thirteenth-century Castile needed its supremacy over León to look ancient rather than recent, and the Arlanza poem, the Crónica najerense and the ballads supplied a founder who had bought his people’s freedom outright. Separating the two is not pedantry: the count who emerges from the charters is a harder and more interesting figure than the one in the poem, because he had to win his position from the king he served rather than receiving it in a bargain over a horse.

keyAchievements.title: One county of Castile
keyAchievements.description: Held Burgos, Lara, Álava, Cerezo and Lantarón together from the early 930s, ending the division of the Leonese eastern march.

keyAchievements.title: The Battle of Simancas, 939
keyAchievements.description: Fought in the coalition that broke Abd al-Rahman III’s great campaign and ended his personal command of armies.

keyAchievements.title: The fuero of Sepúlveda, 940
keyAchievements.description: Repopulated the town beyond the Duero and granted the liberties that became the model for Castilian frontier charters.

keyAchievements.title: A hereditary county
keyAchievements.description: His son García Fernández succeeded him in 970 without a Leonese appointment, turning an office into a dynasty.

timeline.title: First appears as count
timeline.description: Named as count at Lara within the Leonese administration of the eastern frontier; earlier documents giving him the title are suspect.

timeline.title: Count of Castile
timeline.description: A charter of San Pedro de Cardeña of 932 records him as count in Castile under Ramiro II; the counties of Álava, Cerezo and Lantarón came with his marriage to Sancha Sánchez of Pamplona.

timeline.title: Córdoba burns Burgos
timeline.description: Abd al-Rahman III ravaged Álava and Castile and sacked the monastery of Cardeña before being met by the Leonese and Castilians near Osma.

timeline.title: The Battle of Simancas
timeline.description: Fought in the Christian coalition that defeated the caliph’s great muster; the pursuit destroyed his army at the Alhandega.

timeline.title: Repopulates Sepúlveda
timeline.description: Settled the town beyond the Duero and granted it a fuero to attract colonists to the most dangerous ground on the frontier.

timeline.title: Imprisoned by Ramiro II
timeline.description: Rebelled with Diego Muñoz of Saldaña, lost the county to the infante Sancho, and was held in irons at León.

timeline.title: Released and reconciled
timeline.description: Freed on renewed oaths and restored to Castile; his daughter Urraca was married to Ramiro’s heir Ordoño.

timeline.title: Captured by Navarre
timeline.description: Defeated when García Sánchez I of Pamplona intervened for Sancho the Fat, and taken prisoner at Cirueña; freed for territorial concessions.

timeline.title: Terms with al-Hakam II
timeline.description: Made a truce with Córdoba after the destruction of San Esteban de Gormaz, acting independently of the Leonese crown.

timeline.title: Died
timeline.description: Last confirms charters in August 969; his son appears as count on 20 February 970. Buried at San Pedro de Arlanza.

timeline.title: The Poema de Fernán González
timeline.description: A monk of Arlanza gave him the horse and the hawk and the freedom of Castile, three centuries after his death.

succession.note: Castile was a county of the Kingdom of León throughout his life; he never held or claimed a royal title.

predecessor.displayName: Gutier Núñez and the divided counts of the Castilian march
predecessor.note: Castile was not one county before him. After his father Gonzalo Fernández died in 915 the title passed between Fernando Ansúrez, Nuño Fernández and Gutier Núñez, while Álava, Cerezo and Lantarón had counts of their own.

successor.note: His son, count of Castile and Álava from 970 to 995, who inherited without a Leonese appointment — the clearest measure of what his father had actually won.
